  "headline_index": 35,
  "what_the_study_did": "The study performed a simultaneous thrombin and plasmin generation assay (STPGA) to compare human response to a range of species (baboon, Rhesus macaque, swine, rat, rabbit, and guinea pig).",
  "what_it_found": "Non-human primate species (baboon and Rhesus macaque) demonstrated thrombin and plasmin generation that approximated humans more closely than rodents, rabbits, or swine, although significant interspecies differences were still detected.",
  "key_quotes": [
    {
      "quote": "Results are frequently extrapolated to humans; however, data obtained from animal models often falls short of accurate predictions in human response 2.",
      "topic": "Animal model limitations"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Our STPGA assay results suggest that non-human primate species (baboon and rhesus macaque) demonstrated TG and PG that approximated humans more closely than rodents, rabbits or swine.",
      "topic": "Primate similarity"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Nonetheless, within the most comparable species (humans, baboons and rhesus macaques), thrombin and plasmin PH and PR associations were uniquely different (Table 3).",
      "topic": "Interspecies differences"
    },
    {
      "quote": "We show that human fibrinolysis is different from all other species because only human plasmin PH and PR values did not show any association.",
      "topic": "Human fibrinolysis uniqueness"
    },
    {
      "quote": "While the total number of rabbits evaluated were relatively low, the production rates of the first grouping of rabbits (Fig. 3a ) are at least an order of magnitude higher than the second grouping (Fig. 3b ).",
      "topic": "Rabbit PG variability"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Based on the results, we can suggest the following conclusions: Our results provide relevant data on species-dependent blood coagulation and fibrinolysis in a simultaneous TG and PG assay that is conducted on the same plasma sample.",
      "topic": "Species-dependent hemostasis"
    }
  ]
}
